filas.texto: From invoice to price per unit

▸ Price/Unit is what you pay for ONE purchase unit: fees included (a split-case fee, for instance), recoverable tax left out (UK VAT if you're VAT-registered; in the U.S., food bought for resale is usually exempt from sales tax).

▸ Catch weight (meat, fish or cheese billed by actual weight; the invoice line reads 1 case, 50.2 lb × price per lb): buy in lb or kg at the invoice price per lb or kg. The case doesn't matter. The tenderloin on "Recipe Cost Card" is bought this way, at $17.21/lb.

▸ Fixed-weight case that's on the dropdown (50 lb bag, 36x1 lb case, 4x1 gal case, 15 dz case…): pick it as Purchase unit and type the case price exactly as invoiced; the Factor divides it for you. A $29.99 50 lb bag of flour used at 10 oz costs $0.37.

▸ Any other case: read the pack/size on the invoice (4/10 lb = 4 bags of 10 lb = 40 lb; 6/105 oz = six 105 oz cans) and buy in lb, oz, gal or each, with Price/Unit = case price ÷ contents. Say a 6/5 lb case costs $75.00: that's 30 lb, so $2.50/lb. The dropdown won't take a unit that isn't on its list.

▸ #10 cans: the net weight depends on the product (96 to 117 oz, per the USDA Food Buying Guide), so there's no #10 unit. Buy in oz, with Price/Unit = can price ÷ the net weight on the label: a 105 oz can at $5.25 is $0.05 per oz.
▸ Fryer oil is sold by weight (a 35 lb jug-in-box) and shared by everything you fry. Leave it to the Q-factor, or cost it by weight: buy in lb and use in oz, as the Loaded Fries in template 08 does.
Units: what to watch

▸ oz is weight, fl oz is volume. What you buy by weight (lb, oz, kg, g) you use by weight; what you buy by volume (gal, qt, pt, cup, fl oz, L, ml) you use by volume. Crossing over shows '?' and 'check units', on purpose.

▸ U.S. and imperial measures differ. In this kit pt, qt, gal, cup and fl oz are U.S. (1 pt = 473 ml, 1 gal = 3.785 L, 1 fl oz = 29.6 ml). An imperial pint is 568 ml (use imp pt) and a UK fl oz is 28.4 ml; in the UK, work in ml and L.
▸ 'can' on the list is a 12 fl oz (355 ml) beverage can, not a #10 food can (see above).

▸ UK sizes, exactly where: on "Conversions", cell B147 (row bottle→ml, 750: type 700 for a 70 cl bottle) and cell B153 (row can→ml, 355: type 330). Every bottle and can row reads those two cells. It's one size per workbook: if you buy 70 cl spirits and 75 cl wine, keep 'bottle' for the one you use most and cost the other in L.
Yield, cooking loss, scaling and sub-recipes

▸ Your own trim loss: weigh the product as it arrives and again once trimmed; trim loss % = 1 − trimmed weight ÷ AP weight. For whole cuts with trim you reuse (tips, chain, bones for stock), use template 12 (Yield Test): it credits those by-products, so the tenderloin's 39.3% raw loss becomes 37.4% for the card.

▸ Cooking loss: if the quantity on the card is the COOKED portion (a 4 oz cooked patty), trim loss must include what's lost on the heat: 1 − (1 − trim loss) × (1 − cooking loss). The Cooking Loss Test tab of template 12 does the math. Or simply enter the raw weight.

▸ Scaling: conversion factor = new yield ÷ old yield. Multiply every Quantity by it and set Number of portions to the new yield (from 10 to 25: factor 2.5, so 3 lb becomes 7.5 lb). Cost per portion doesn't change; the total does. Duplicate the tab first (right-click the tab → Move or Copy → Create a copy).

▸ Sub-recipes (stocks, sauces, doughs): cost the batch on its own card (a copy of the tab) with Number of portions = the batch yield in the unit you'll use (e.g., 6 qt) and Q-factor at 0%, so it isn't counted twice. On the main card, buy it in that unit: in Price/Unit type = and click the sub-recipe's COST PER PORTION. The dark veal stock on "Recipe Cost Card" ($10.00 a quart) is a placeholder for exactly that.

▸ Weigh dry goods. The kit never converts volume to weight: a cup of flour weighs more or less depending on how it's filled. Enter flour, sugar and the like in oz or g; if a recipe says cups, weigh one cup of YOUR product once and use that weight. Pinches of salt and spices: weigh them or leave them to the Q-factor.
▸ Keep your prices in template 13 (Ingredient Price Tracker): it flags any ingredient that has gone up more than 5% since your cards were costed, so you know which cards to update.
Tax by market: what to type and what to print
▸ U.S.: leave Tax rate (%) at 0%. Print the pre-tax suggested price; sales tax is added to the check (about 7.5% on average, state plus local). In Current menu price, type the price as printed.

▸ UK: set 20% (VAT) and print the price incl. tax, since UK menus show VAT-inclusive prices. In Current menu price, type your menu price WITHOUT VAT, dividing by 1.20 rather than subtracting 20%: £18.00 on the menu is 15.00, not 14.40. Your GP % is 100% minus the actual food cost %.
▸ Canada: as in the U.S., menus show prices before GST/HST (5-15%): leave 0%, or type your rate to see what the guest pays.
▸ Australia: set 10% (GST) and print the price incl. tax; in Current menu price, type the menu price ÷ 1.10.
▸ Tips and service charges are never part of the price you cost against.

Pours, pour cost and bar taxes
▸ U.S. standard pours: spirits 1.5 fl oz · wine 5 fl oz · beer 12 fl oz (bottle or can) · draft beer, usually a 16 fl oz pint.

▸ UK legal measures: gin, rum, vodka and whisky in 25 ml or 35 ml (or multiples) · still wine by the glass in 125 ml or 175 ml (or multiples) · draft beer and cider in ⅓, ½ or ⅔ pint, or multiples of ½ pint. Pour in ml, and in imp pt for beer.
▸ Spirits: buy in L (price per liter from "Bottle Sizes"), pour in fl oz (UK: ml). Pour cost 18-20%.
▸ Wine by the glass: the same, from its 750 ml row on "Bottle Sizes" (or by the 12x750 ml case). Its pour cost runs higher than spirits.

▸ Draft beer: buy in 1/6 bbl keg, 1/2 bbl keg or 50 L keg at the keg price, pour in fl oz (UK: imp pt). About 20%. A $110 sixtel poured in 16 fl oz pints costs $2.66 a pint before foam and line loss: put those in Trim loss %.
▸ Bottled and canned beer: buy by the 'can' or the 24x12 fl oz case, sell by the can. About 25%.

▸ Aperol Spritz: the example uses a 1.5 fl oz house pour of Aperol. The classic 3-2-1 spec (3 parts prosecco, 2 Aperol, 1 soda) takes 2 fl oz and runs about 28% pour cost at $15: spritzes are wine-based and cost more than a spirit-forward drink.
▸ Whole bar: 18-24% pour cost, which a UK bar reads as 76-82% GP. To cost a beer or a glass of wine, duplicate a cocktail tab (right-click the tab → Move or Copy → Create a copy).

▸ Taxes the bar pays on its drink sales come off the price before you judge pour cost. Texas, for example, charges the permit holder 6.7% of mixed-drink receipts, on top of the 8.25% sales tax the guest pays: for a $14.00 margarita, type 13.06 in Current menu price (14.00 × 0.933).
